1	# S111 Avida: how the three properties will be measured, written before running
2	
3	*Log S111, decision S59. Written on 29 September 2026 by one Opus 5.5 agent (S56), and committed **before any measuring run**. The only runs made before this file: the build, and one timing run (the default ancestor, seed 1, 3,000 updates, 104 seconds; its numbers are used below only to choose run lengths). Nothing in the theory's text, formal core, claims or program is touched by this work.*
4	
5	## 0. What is being asked
6	
7	The owner (S59): knowledge is information that "Can cause itself to be copied", "Can cause itself to resist change" and "Can cause itself to remain"; the owner asked for "a type of program with these exact properties". Claude named digital organisms and proposed to measure the three properties on Avida's organisms: a working case of knowledge without explanation, to build from. The owner: "Yup do the next step please."
8	
9	Avida (Ofria and colleagues, Michigan State University) is a research simulator. Its organisms are short programs, each a list of instructions from a set of 26, run on a simulated processor inside a simulated world. An organism that copies its instructions into new memory and splits off the copy has an offspring. The world is a 60 by 60 grid; an offspring goes into a neighbouring cell, replacing whoever was there. Everything below runs inside Avida; nothing that copies itself runs on the real machine.
10	
11	Throughout, the question for each measure is also **what causes it: the organism's own instructions, or the simulated world** (the scheduler that hands out processor time, the memory, the mutations the world applies when an instruction is copied, the removal of organisms when space runs short or when they grow old).
12	
13	## 1. The setup
14	
15	- **Avida** 2.14.0 at commit 47f13dad (github.com/devosoft/avida), with its library `libs/apto` at the pinned commit 02e18980; built in the scratch space with cmake and make, release build, the environment variable `AVIDA_DISABLE_BACKTRACE=1` (so the `libs/backward-cpp` library is not needed). No patch and no extra compiler flag were needed with g++ 13.3.0 (285 compiler warnings, no errors). The build notes go into `results/S111 Avida - the runs/`.
16	- **Ancestor**: Avida's default hand-written organism, `default-heads.org`, 100 instructions: a 5-instruction head (make room for the copy; find the end), 85 filler instructions (`nop-C`, doing nothing but able to be changed), and a 10-instruction copy loop (copy one instruction; check whether the end is reached; if so, split off the copy; if not, go back). Written as letters (one letter per instruction), it is `wzcag` + 85 × `c` + `zvfcaxgab`.
17	- **World**: Avida's default configuration (`avida.cfg`), except the copy error rate and the seed, and the output events below. Default: 60 × 60 cells on a torus; the offspring goes to a random neighbouring cell (an empty one first); an organism dies after executing 20 times its length in instructions; one instruction inserted with probability 0.05 and one deleted with probability 0.05 at each split; processor time handed out in proportion to "merit" (the organism's length executed, multiplied by the rewards for tasks).
18	- **Environment**: the default `environment.cfg`: nine logic tasks on two 32-bit numbers the world supplies (NOT, NAND, AND, OR-NOT, OR, AND-NOT, NOR, XOR, EQU), each rewarded with extra processor time, once per life each.
19	- **Conditions**, three copy error rates (the chance that each instruction copied is replaced by a random one): **low 0.0025**, **default 0.0075** (Avida's own), **high 0.02**; for the ancestor's 100 instructions, about 0.25, 0.75 and 2.0 copy errors per offspring. **Three seeds per condition** (1, 2, 3): nine runs.
20	- **Run length**: 50,000 updates each (an update is Avida's unit of time: about 30 instructions executed per organism). From the timing run, about 29 updates a second, so about 30 minutes a run; three runs at a time; each under a timeout of 2 hours. About 3,500 to 4,000 generations. If a run is cut by its timeout, its last saved state is used and the shortfall recorded.
21	- **Saved**: every 1,000 updates, the counts (organisms, births, births with an offspring identical to its parent, Avida's `num_breed_true`), the tasks performed, the dominant (most common) genotype, the average generation; the whole population (every genotype with its count and sequence) at updates 1,000, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000, 40,000 and 50,000.
22	- **Test processor**: Avida's analysis mode runs a program alone in a private processor, with no mutations and no neighbours. There Avida calls a program **viable** when it produces an offspring identical to itself (or one that, run in turn, cycles back to it). "Fitness" there is merit divided by the time taken to copy. Every knockout and mutant is judged there.
23	- **Knockout**: one instruction replaced by `nop-X`, an instruction that does nothing and, unlike `nop-C`, is not read as part of a label. `nop-X` is added, as a 27th instruction, only to the instruction set of the analysis runs and of the control worlds, never to the main runs.
24	
25	## 2. COPIED: information that can cause itself to be copied
26	
27	**Measures.**
28	- C1. The ancestor in the test processor: viable or not; instructions executed per copy; length copied.
29	- C2. **Knockout test on the ancestor**: each of the 100 instructions in turn replaced by `nop-X`; for each, viable or not. The sites whose knockout stops self-copying are the **essential sites**; the rest are the **non-essential sites**.
30	- C3. **Copy fidelity** at each error rate: (i) expected share of offspring identical to the parent, from the rates and the length; (ii) Avida's `SAMPLE_OFFSPRING`, 1,000 offspring of the ancestor made in the test processor under each condition's rates, the share identical to the parent; (iii) in the world, births with the offspring identical to the parent divided by all births, per run, averaged over updates 1,000 to 50,000.
31	- C4. **Offspring per organism**: in the world, births per organism per update, and the average generation reached at 50,000 updates; for comparison, the ancestor alone in the test processor.
32	- C5. From one injected ancestor, the population size over time.
33	
34	**Counts as the property shown**: the ancestor is viable; a population grows from one injected ancestor; the knockouts split into a small set that stops copying and a large set that does not, and the small set is the instructions that ask for the copy (room, copy, split) and the labels that steer them.
35	**Counts against**: the ancestor is not viable; copying survives every knockout (then the copying would be the world's doing, whatever the program says); every knockout stops it (then nothing in the program marks what matters); random programs copy as often as the ancestor (control K1).
36	**Program or world**: the program's instructions ask for each step (`h-alloc` room, `h-copy` one instruction, `h-divide` split); the simulated processor carries each out, and the world supplies the time and places the offspring. The knockout test shows which part the program contributes: without those instructions the world copies nothing. Fidelity is set by the world: the program has no instruction that checks or repairs a copy against its original (checked by reading the instruction set; `if-label` compares the last copied instructions with a label, to find the end).
37	
38	## 3. RESISTS CHANGE: information that can cause itself to resist change
39	
40	Two senses are kept apart: (a) **what the program does** stays the same when its instructions change (robustness); (b) **the instructions themselves** stay the same in the population (conservation).
41	
42	**(a) By its own structure: mutational robustness.**
43	- R1. For the dominant genotype of each run at updates 10,000, 30,000 and 50,000, and for the ancestor: **every single-point mutant** (each site replaced by each of the 25 other instructions of the set). For each mutant, in the test processor: viable or not; fitness. Shares reported: viable (still copies itself exactly); **neutral** (viable and fitness within one part in a million of the unmutated genotype's); lethal (not viable).
44	- R2. The shares compared between the low and the high error rate (three seeds each; the default rate between). Wilke and colleagues (2001), from memory and not checked here, reported that at a high error rate a population can come to favour genomes whose mutants lose less ("survival of the flattest"); **only these runs are used**, not that paper: the comparison either shows a higher neutral share at the high rate or it does not.
45	
46	**(b) By the population: conservation.**
47	- R3. At each saved population (1,000 to 50,000), every genotype is aligned to the ancestor (a global alignment, one point for a match, minus one for a mismatch or a gap). For each ancestral site, the share of organisms (weighted by count) whose aligned instruction is the ancestor's. **Averaged over the essential sites and over the non-essential sites (from C2) separately.**
48	- R4. The same share in the no-mutation control (K5): the baseline where the world changes nothing.
49	
50	**Counts as shown**: (a) a large share of single changes leave copying and fitness unchanged; the comparison tells whether the share moves with the error rate. (b) Essential sites stay the ancestor's in a larger share of the population than non-essential sites, at the same error rate.
51	**Counts against**: (a) most single changes stop copying; (b) essential and non-essential sites change at the same pace (the world's changes are not being undone).
52	**Program or world**: no instruction repairs anything. In (a), what buffers change is the arrangement of the program's instructions (which sites matter); that arrangement was itself shaped by which variants the world let persist. In (b), what keeps essential sites unchanged is the world: a variant that cannot copy leaves no offspring and dies of age or is overwritten; the program's part is only that its essential sites are the ones whose change stops copying.
53	
54	## 4. REMAINS: information that can cause itself to remain
55	
56	- M1. Population size over time in every run (above zero to the end or not).
57	- M2. **Persistence of the essential information**: at each saved population, the share of organisms carrying the ancestor's copy loop `zvfcaxgab` and its head `wzcag` exactly (anywhere in the genome); the essential-site conservation of R3; the share carrying the whole ancestral genome.
58	- M3. Generations elapsed; the ancestor's lineage (every organism descends from the one injected).
59	
60	**Controls that should not remain** (each alone in a default world unless stated; one seed; 2,000 updates):
61	- K1. **Random programs**: 10,000 random genomes of length 100 (each instruction drawn evenly from the 26) tested in the test processor for viability; and 100 of them injected into the world, one per cell, followed.
62	- K2. **The ancestor with its copy loop knocked out** (`h-copy` replaced by `nop-X`): tested in the test processor; injected alone, followed.
63	- K3. K2 in a world where **nothing dies of age** (Avida's `DEATH_METHOD 0`): expected to remain, showing that when nothing removes it, a program that cannot copy remains too; remaining is then the world's doing.
64	- K4. K2 and the intact ancestor injected side by side, nothing dying of age: whether the non-copier is removed by the copier's offspring taking the space.
65	- K5. **No mutation**: the ancestor, error rates all set to 0, 5,000 updates, one seed: the baseline for R3 and M2.
66	
67	**Counts as shown**: the populations last to 50,000 updates; the essential information is present in most organisms at every save; K1 and K2 vanish in the default world.
68	**Counts against**: runs die out; the essential information is lost; the controls remain as long as the copiers in the default world.
69	**Program or world**: the world removes (old age, overwriting); what remains is what is copied faster than it is removed. The program's part is the copying (section 2); K3 separates it from the world's removal rule.
70	
71	## 5. Marletto's test on something beyond copying
72	
73	The test, as file S110 quotes it: knowledge "is exactly the thing one would ultimately have to eliminate in order to prevent a particular transformation from being performed reliably." (Marletto, ch. 5)
74	
75	**Applied only if logic tasks evolve.** For each run whose population performs any task at 50,000 updates, and for each task performed by at least 10% of the organisms there:
76	- T1. In the dominant genotype: each instruction knocked out in turn; the sites whose knockout stops the task (and whether copying survives).
77	- T2. **One copy against every copy**: the share of the population performing the task (weighted by count, each genotype run in the test processor) (i) as found; (ii) with the task's sites knocked out in the dominant genotype only; (iii) with each of the most common genotypes (together at least 90% of the organisms, at most 300 genotypes) given its own knockout map and all of its own task sites knocked out at once.
78	- Reported: how many and which instructions (e.g. `nand`, `IO`) one would have to eliminate, and whether eliminating them in one genotype stops the population performing the task reliably, or only eliminating them in every copy does.
79	**Counts against the test picking something out**: no knockout stops the task (it would be done by something other than the program), or eliminating it in one genotype already stops the population.
80	**Program or world**: the program's instructions compute the function (read inputs, `nand`, write output); the world supplies the inputs, checks the output and pays for it in processor time.
81	
82	## 6. Replicates, summaries, what is not measured
83	
84	- Every number over seeds is given per seed and as the mean with the smallest and largest. With three seeds a difference is called a difference only if every seed of one condition lies beyond every seed of the other; otherwise "no clear difference".
85	- Not measured: insertion and deletion mutants in the robustness scan (point changes only); competition between evolved genotypes (the design of Wilke and colleagues); anything about explanation, problems or criticism (the next kind, S59).
86	- Scripts in `Semantics/tools/` named in plain words; configurations, exact commands and summary tables in `results/S111 Avida - the runs/`; raw output only in the scratch space.
87	- Any departure from this plan is recorded in the results file with its reason.

# S111 Avida: how the three properties will be measured, written before running

*Log S111, decision S59. Written on 29 September 2026 by one Opus 5.5 agent (S56), and committed **before any measuring run**. The only runs made before this file: the build, and one timing run (the default ancestor, seed 1, 3,000 updates, 104 seconds; its numbers are used below only to choose run lengths). Nothing in the theory's text, formal core, claims or program is touched by this work.*

## 0. What is being asked

The owner (S59): knowledge is information that "Can cause itself to be copied", "Can cause itself to resist change" and "Can cause itself to remain"; the owner asked for "a type of program with these exact properties". Claude named digital organisms and proposed to measure the three properties on Avida's organisms: a working case of knowledge without explanation, to build from. The owner: "Yup do the next step please."

Avida (Ofria and colleagues, Michigan State University) is a research simulator. Its organisms are short programs, each a list of instructions from a set of 26, run on a simulated processor inside a simulated world. An organism that copies its instructions into new memory and splits off the copy has an offspring. The world is a 60 by 60 grid; an offspring goes into a neighbouring cell, replacing whoever was there. Everything below runs inside Avida; nothing that copies itself runs on the real machine.

Throughout, the question for each measure is also **what causes it: the organism's own instructions, or the simulated world** (the scheduler that hands out processor time, the memory, the mutations the world applies when an instruction is copied, the removal of organisms when space runs short or when they grow old).

## 1. The setup

- **Avida** 2.14.0 at commit 47f13dad (github.com/devosoft/avida), with its library `libs/apto` at the pinned commit 02e18980; built in the scratch space with cmake and make, release build, the environment variable `AVIDA_DISABLE_BACKTRACE=1` (so the `libs/backward-cpp` library is not needed). No patch and no extra compiler flag were needed with g++ 13.3.0 (285 compiler warnings, no errors). The build notes go into `results/S111 Avida - the runs/`.
- **Ancestor**: Avida's default hand-written organism, `default-heads.org`, 100 instructions: a 5-instruction head (make room for the copy; find the end), 85 filler instructions (`nop-C`, doing nothing but able to be changed), and a 10-instruction copy loop (copy one instruction; check whether the end is reached; if so, split off the copy; if not, go back). Written as letters (one letter per instruction), it is `wzcag` + 85 × `c` + `zvfcaxgab`.
- **World**: Avida's default configuration (`avida.cfg`), except the copy error rate and the seed, and the output events below. Default: 60 × 60 cells on a torus; the offspring goes to a random neighbouring cell (an empty one first); an organism dies after executing 20 times its length in instructions; one instruction inserted with probability 0.05 and one deleted with probability 0.05 at each split; processor time handed out in proportion to "merit" (the organism's length executed, multiplied by the rewards for tasks).
- **Environment**: the default `environment.cfg`: nine logic tasks on two 32-bit numbers the world supplies (NOT, NAND, AND, OR-NOT, OR, AND-NOT, NOR, XOR, EQU), each rewarded with extra processor time, once per life each.
- **Conditions**, three copy error rates (the chance that each instruction copied is replaced by a random one): **low 0.0025**, **default 0.0075** (Avida's own), **high 0.02**; for the ancestor's 100 instructions, about 0.25, 0.75 and 2.0 copy errors per offspring. **Three seeds per condition** (1, 2, 3): nine runs.
- **Run length**: 50,000 updates each (an update is Avida's unit of time: about 30 instructions executed per organism). From the timing run, about 29 updates a second, so about 30 minutes a run; three runs at a time; each under a timeout of 2 hours. About 3,500 to 4,000 generations. If a run is cut by its timeout, its last saved state is used and the shortfall recorded.
- **Saved**: every 1,000 updates, the counts (organisms, births, births with an offspring identical to its parent, Avida's `num_breed_true`), the tasks performed, the dominant (most common) genotype, the average generation; the whole population (every genotype with its count and sequence) at updates 1,000, 10,000, 20,000, 30,000, 40,000 and 50,000.
- **Test processor**: Avida's analysis mode runs a program alone in a private processor, with no mutations and no neighbours. There Avida calls a program **viable** when it produces an offspring identical to itself (or one that, run in turn, cycles back to it). "Fitness" there is merit divided by the time taken to copy. Every knockout and mutant is judged there.
- **Knockout**: one instruction replaced by `nop-X`, an instruction that does nothing and, unlike `nop-C`, is not read as part of a label. `nop-X` is added, as a 27th instruction, only to the instruction set of the analysis runs and of the control worlds, never to the main runs.

## 2. COPIED: information that can cause itself to be copied

**Measures.**
- C1. The ancestor in the test processor: viable or not; instructions executed per copy; length copied.
- C2. **Knockout test on the ancestor**: each of the 100 instructions in turn replaced by `nop-X`; for each, viable or not. The sites whose knockout stops self-copying are the **essential sites**; the rest are the **non-essential sites**.
- C3. **Copy fidelity** at each error rate: (i) expected share of offspring identical to the parent, from the rates and the length; (ii) Avida's `SAMPLE_OFFSPRING`, 1,000 offspring of the ancestor made in the test processor under each condition's rates, the share identical to the parent; (iii) in the world, births with the offspring identical to the parent divided by all births, per run, averaged over updates 1,000 to 50,000.
- C4. **Offspring per organism**: in the world, births per organism per update, and the average generation reached at 50,000 updates; for comparison, the ancestor alone in the test processor.
- C5. From one injected ancestor, the population size over time.

**Counts as the property shown**: the ancestor is viable; a population grows from one injected ancestor; the knockouts split into a small set that stops copying and a large set that does not, and the small set is the instructions that ask for the copy (room, copy, split) and the labels that steer them.
**Counts against**: the ancestor is not viable; copying survives every knockout (then the copying would be the world's doing, whatever the program says); every knockout stops it (then nothing in the program marks what matters); random programs copy as often as the ancestor (control K1).
**Program or world**: the program's instructions ask for each step (`h-alloc` room, `h-copy` one instruction, `h-divide` split); the simulated processor carries each out, and the world supplies the time and places the offspring. The knockout test shows which part the program contributes: without those instructions the world copies nothing. Fidelity is set by the world: the program has no instruction that checks or repairs a copy against its original (checked by reading the instruction set; `if-label` compares the last copied instructions with a label, to find the end).

## 3. RESISTS CHANGE: information that can cause itself to resist change

Two senses are kept apart: (a) **what the program does** stays the same when its instructions change (robustness); (b) **the instructions themselves** stay the same in the population (conservation).

**(a) By its own structure: mutational robustness.**
- R1. For the dominant genotype of each run at updates 10,000, 30,000 and 50,000, and for the ancestor: **every single-point mutant** (each site replaced by each of the 25 other instructions of the set). For each mutant, in the test processor: viable or not; fitness. Shares reported: viable (still copies itself exactly); **neutral** (viable and fitness within one part in a million of the unmutated genotype's); lethal (not viable).
- R2. The shares compared between the low and the high error rate (three seeds each; the default rate between). Wilke and colleagues (2001), from memory and not checked here, reported that at a high error rate a population can come to favour genomes whose mutants lose less ("survival of the flattest"); **only these runs are used**, not that paper: the comparison either shows a higher neutral share at the high rate or it does not.

**(b) By the population: conservation.**
- R3. At each saved population (1,000 to 50,000), every genotype is aligned to the ancestor (a global alignment, one point for a match, minus one for a mismatch or a gap). For each ancestral site, the share of organisms (weighted by count) whose aligned instruction is the ancestor's. **Averaged over the essential sites and over the non-essential sites (from C2) separately.**
- R4. The same share in the no-mutation control (K5): the baseline where the world changes nothing.

**Counts as shown**: (a) a large share of single changes leave copying and fitness unchanged; the comparison tells whether the share moves with the error rate. (b) Essential sites stay the ancestor's in a larger share of the population than non-essential sites, at the same error rate.
**Counts against**: (a) most single changes stop copying; (b) essential and non-essential sites change at the same pace (the world's changes are not being undone).
**Program or world**: no instruction repairs anything. In (a), what buffers change is the arrangement of the program's instructions (which sites matter); that arrangement was itself shaped by which variants the world let persist. In (b), what keeps essential sites unchanged is the world: a variant that cannot copy leaves no offspring and dies of age or is overwritten; the program's part is only that its essential sites are the ones whose change stops copying.

## 4. REMAINS: information that can cause itself to remain

- M1. Population size over time in every run (above zero to the end or not).
- M2. **Persistence of the essential information**: at each saved population, the share of organisms carrying the ancestor's copy loop `zvfcaxgab` and its head `wzcag` exactly (anywhere in the genome); the essential-site conservation of R3; the share carrying the whole ancestral genome.
- M3. Generations elapsed; the ancestor's lineage (every organism descends from the one injected).

**Controls that should not remain** (each alone in a default world unless stated; one seed; 2,000 updates):
- K1. **Random programs**: 10,000 random genomes of length 100 (each instruction drawn evenly from the 26) tested in the test processor for viability; and 100 of them injected into the world, one per cell, followed.
- K2. **The ancestor with its copy loop knocked out** (`h-copy` replaced by `nop-X`): tested in the test processor; injected alone, followed.
- K3. K2 in a world where **nothing dies of age** (Avida's `DEATH_METHOD 0`): expected to remain, showing that when nothing removes it, a program that cannot copy remains too; remaining is then the world's doing.
- K4. K2 and the intact ancestor injected side by side, nothing dying of age: whether the non-copier is removed by the copier's offspring taking the space.
- K5. **No mutation**: the ancestor, error rates all set to 0, 5,000 updates, one seed: the baseline for R3 and M2.

**Counts as shown**: the populations last to 50,000 updates; the essential information is present in most organisms at every save; K1 and K2 vanish in the default world.
**Counts against**: runs die out; the essential information is lost; the controls remain as long as the copiers in the default world.
**Program or world**: the world removes (old age, overwriting); what remains is what is copied faster than it is removed. The program's part is the copying (section 2); K3 separates it from the world's removal rule.

## 5. Marletto's test on something beyond copying

The test, as file S110 quotes it: knowledge "is exactly the thing one would ultimately have to eliminate in order to prevent a particular transformation from being performed reliably." (Marletto, ch. 5)

**Applied only if logic tasks evolve.** For each run whose population performs any task at 50,000 updates, and for each task performed by at least 10% of the organisms there:
- T1. In the dominant genotype: each instruction knocked out in turn; the sites whose knockout stops the task (and whether copying survives).
- T2. **One copy against every copy**: the share of the population performing the task (weighted by count, each genotype run in the test processor) (i) as found; (ii) with the task's sites knocked out in the dominant genotype only; (iii) with each of the most common genotypes (together at least 90% of the organisms, at most 300 genotypes) given its own knockout map and all of its own task sites knocked out at once.
- Reported: how many and which instructions (e.g. `nand`, `IO`) one would have to eliminate, and whether eliminating them in one genotype stops the population performing the task reliably, or only eliminating them in every copy does.
**Counts against the test picking something out**: no knockout stops the task (it would be done by something other than the program), or eliminating it in one genotype already stops the population.
**Program or world**: the program's instructions compute the function (read inputs, `nand`, write output); the world supplies the inputs, checks the output and pays for it in processor time.

## 6. Replicates, summaries, what is not measured

- Every number over seeds is given per seed and as the mean with the smallest and largest. With three seeds a difference is called a difference only if every seed of one condition lies beyond every seed of the other; otherwise "no clear difference".
- Not measured: insertion and deletion mutants in the robustness scan (point changes only); competition between evolved genotypes (the design of Wilke and colleagues); anything about explanation, problems or criticism (the next kind, S59).
- Scripts in `Semantics/tools/` named in plain words; configurations, exact commands and summary tables in `results/S111 Avida - the runs/`; raw output only in the scratch space.
- Any departure from this plan is recorded in the results file with its reason.

1	# S111 Avida: how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending
2	
3	*Written 29 September 2026 by the one Opus 5.5 agent that did the whole S111 job under decision S56 (the plan, the runs, the measures, the results and the plain-words file), before anything of this cross-examination was built or sent. When this file was committed, the returns folder `results/S111 Avida - GLM cross-examination returns/` did not exist, no brief or manifest had been built, no call had been sent and no runner of it was going. It follows log S110's cross-examination rule (`results/S110 - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md`) where it says nothing else. It obeys decision S23 except where it quotes the owner; for what the theory judges it says "candidate" or "explanation", never "model" (S43).*
4	
5	*Amended once before sending, 29 September 2026, by the same agent, after a first build that was deleted unsent and uncommitted: the sandboxes also hold the seventh script, `tools/s111_summarise_the_three_properties.py`, which gathers the numbers of the results' `.json`; "six" became "seven" below. Nothing else changed.*
6	
7	## The instruction
8	
9	- **S56**, the owner's words: "It's capable of doing the whole thing on its own. Use GLM for cross examination." So one Opus agent did the whole S111 job, and GLM cross-examines it in place of a fresh Opus critical reviewer.
10	- **S59**: the job itself: the owner's three properties of knowledge (information that can cause itself to be copied, to resist change, to remain), measured on Avida's digital organisms, a working case of knowledge without explanation; the explanation kind comes next. Part B stays held before its settlement (S57); nothing of Part B, and nothing of S110, is sent, opened or written.
11	- **S39, S29, S17**: up to four GLM calls at once, each through Claude Code, at medium effort. **S20, S21, S23, S28, S43**: the owner's words bind every finding as content.
12	
13	## What is sent
14	
15	Four jobs, built by `tools/s111x_build.py` (Part A round 1's build imported for its helpers only; the sandboxed helper `tools/glm_via_claude_code_sandboxed.py` and the shell guard `tools/glm_sandbox_shell_guard.py` used unchanged), run by `tools/s111x_glm_loop.py` (log S110's cross-examination runner with its names changed):
16	
17	| job | tag | angle |
18	|---|---|---|
19	| 1 | `s111x_glm_a` | (a) whether the measures measure the three properties as the owner stated them |
20	| 2 | `s111x_glm_b` | (b) the scripts and the numbers |
21	| 3 | `s111x_glm_c` | (c) what the program causes and what the simulated world does |
22	| 4 | `s111x_glm_d` | (d) the plain-words file against the results |
23	
24	Each sandbox holds copies only: the plan written before running; the results (`.md`, `.json`); the plain-words file 111; this rule; Avida's configuration files as used; the build notes with Avida's rules as read from its source; the exact commands; the four summary tables (`.md`, `.json`); the seven S111 scripts (six measuring scripts and the one that gathers the results' numbers). Job 1 adds the decisions record and the two S110 records that give Marletto's test; job 4 adds the decisions record and plain file 110 (for style). **No sandbox holds Avida's source or binary, or any raw run output**: those stay in the scratch space, and the build refuses any source outside `Semantics/`. There is no program in any sandbox (no `model/` folder), so the guard refuses every command: GLM may Read, Glob and Grep, and writes nothing. Each brief quotes the owner's words (S19, S20, S21, S23, S28, S43, S56, S57, S59) and asks for objections, each with **the exact fix**, terse, at most about 3,000 words, last line `END OF REPORT`. The briefs, manifests and job list are named, with their md5s, in `tools/s111x_jobs - S111, GLM cross-examination.json`, written by the build and committed before the launch.
25	
26	- **The call**: glm-5.3 through Claude Code (S29), `--effort medium` (S17), the 1,000,000-token window, 6 attempts, at most 3 answers without END OF REPORT, 7,200 seconds per attempt, `--rule` (this file, committed and unchanged from HEAD), `--brief-md5`, `--manifest-md5`. Up to 3 passes per job. Sandboxes in `<scratchpad>/s111x_sandboxes/`, homes in `<scratchpad>/s111x_homes/`. Returns in `results/S111 Avida - GLM cross-examination returns/`.
27	- **Before the launch**: a dry test of the four sandboxes with a dummy key (built by the helper's own `build_sandbox`; the guard handed a write, `touch`, two `python3 -c`, `cat`, `env`, a redirect and a run of one of the S111 scripts, each to be refused; every sandbox to come back unchanged; no Avida binary, no `.spop` or `.dat` file, no file larger than the summaries), recorded and committed; S110's GLM run (session leader PID 6632) must have exited (`kill -0 6632` fails), so that no more than four GLM calls run at once.
28	
29	## How the replies will be read
30	
31	1. **Nothing is opened until all four calls end.** No reply, receipt, reasoning file, attempt file, stream file or guard log of this cross-examination is opened until every job has ended its last allowed pass: the run log holds `s111x_glm_loop: every pass ended; …` and `loop ended <UTC time>`, and the process in the pid file has exited. The progress lines may be watched; they hold no reply text. If a call is still running 24 hours after the launch, the runner may be stopped by its PID and the calls not ended recorded as not returned.
32	2. **What counts as a reply**: only `<tag>.response.txt` (or `<tag>_pass<k>.response.txt`); failed calls count neither way; connection failures are not answers; a key in the output or a sandbox not unchanged is reported before anything else is read.
33	3. **One Opus agent reads every objection and settles each**, by argument from the plan, the results, the scripts, the configuration and Avida's source, or **by rerunning** (Avida, the scripts, or a new check) in the scratch space, never in the repository; and records for each: the objection, its settlement (stands, stands in part, does not stand), the reason (or the rerun and its numbers), and what it changes. An objection is a claim until settled; an objection repeated by several jobs decides nothing (arguments, not numbers); silence is not agreement. The agent writes `results/S111 Avida - the GLM cross-examination, settled.md`, created at once and filled as it goes.
34	4. **Findings that stand amend the S111 files in corrected copies**: `… , after the cross-examination.md` (and `.json`) beside the results file, and corrected copies of any summary table or script that changes (a script's corrected copy gets its own plain name and note); the files as sent are kept as they were. The plain-words file 111 is updated to match, and its note says it now follows the check. Nothing in the theory's text, formal core, claims or program, any Part A, Part B or S110 file, the decisions record or `authority/` is written.
35	5. **The owner's words bind every finding as content** (S20 to S59). An objection that would settle for the owner something the S111 files leave open (whether these organisms hold knowledge; how the three properties should be read; what the explanation kind needs) is recorded, not applied (S28, S21). No finding ranks anything (S20).
36	6. **Records** follow the settlement, by the same agent: an addition to log S111 in the project story and the plain story, and Status, INDEX and README as earlier entries did. Then the owner chooses the next step.
37	
38	## How the run is launched
39	
40	From the repository root, after this file's commit is pushed and the build and dry test are committed, once `kill -0 6632` fails, one process, detached so that it outlives the agent that starts it, with the key loaded only into its own environment from the session's key file and never opened or printed by the agent, and the other keys unset:
41	
42	```
43	setsid nohup bash -c 'cd /home/user/ThreadSmith || exit 1; echo "launched $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"; R="Semantics/results/S111 Avida - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md"; { git ls-files --error-unmatch -- "$R" >/dev/null && git diff --quiet HEAD -- "$R"; } || { echo "the reading rule is not committed or differs from HEAD; nothing sent"; exit 1; }; set -a; . <key file>; set +a; unset ATRIA_API_KEY MIMO_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY; python3 -B Semantics/tools/s111x_glm_loop.py "Semantics/tools/s111x_jobs - S111, GLM cross-examination.json"; echo "loop ended $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"' > <scratchpad>/s111x_glm_run.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
44	```
45	
46	The process id of the session leader goes in `<scratchpad>/s111x_glm_run.pid`. The launching agent writes `results/S111 Avida - GLM cross-examination, launch record.md`, commits it, and hands back once the log shows all four calls sent.
47	
48	## Unsure
49	
50	- GLM cannot run Avida or see the raw output; it judges the numbers by their consistency with the scripts, the configuration and each other. A claim it cannot check is to be listed as not reached, not as an objection.
51	- GLM sees Avida's rules only as the build notes give them, with source lines; a rule misread there could pass unnoticed.
52	- One GLM job per angle may miss what the work also missed.
53

# S111 Avida: how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending

*Written 29 September 2026 by the one Opus 5.5 agent that did the whole S111 job under decision S56 (the plan, the runs, the measures, the results and the plain-words file), before anything of this cross-examination was built or sent. When this file was committed, the returns folder `results/S111 Avida - GLM cross-examination returns/` did not exist, no brief or manifest had been built, no call had been sent and no runner of it was going. It follows log S110's cross-examination rule (`results/S110 - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md`) where it says nothing else. It obeys decision S23 except where it quotes the owner; for what the theory judges it says "candidate" or "explanation", never "model" (S43).*

*Amended once before sending, 29 September 2026, by the same agent, after a first build that was deleted unsent and uncommitted: the sandboxes also hold the seventh script, `tools/s111_summarise_the_three_properties.py`, which gathers the numbers of the results' `.json`; "six" became "seven" below. Nothing else changed.*

## The instruction

- **S56**, the owner's words: "It's capable of doing the whole thing on its own. Use GLM for cross examination." So one Opus agent did the whole S111 job, and GLM cross-examines it in place of a fresh Opus critical reviewer.
- **S59**: the job itself: the owner's three properties of knowledge (information that can cause itself to be copied, to resist change, to remain), measured on Avida's digital organisms, a working case of knowledge without explanation; the explanation kind comes next. Part B stays held before its settlement (S57); nothing of Part B, and nothing of S110, is sent, opened or written.
- **S39, S29, S17**: up to four GLM calls at once, each through Claude Code, at medium effort. **S20, S21, S23, S28, S43**: the owner's words bind every finding as content.

## What is sent

Four jobs, built by `tools/s111x_build.py` (Part A round 1's build imported for its helpers only; the sandboxed helper `tools/glm_via_claude_code_sandboxed.py` and the shell guard `tools/glm_sandbox_shell_guard.py` used unchanged), run by `tools/s111x_glm_loop.py` (log S110's cross-examination runner with its names changed):

| job | tag | angle |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `s111x_glm_a` | (a) whether the measures measure the three properties as the owner stated them |
| 2 | `s111x_glm_b` | (b) the scripts and the numbers |
| 3 | `s111x_glm_c` | (c) what the program causes and what the simulated world does |
| 4 | `s111x_glm_d` | (d) the plain-words file against the results |

Each sandbox holds copies only: the plan written before running; the results (`.md`, `.json`); the plain-words file 111; this rule; Avida's configuration files as used; the build notes with Avida's rules as read from its source; the exact commands; the four summary tables (`.md`, `.json`); the seven S111 scripts (six measuring scripts and the one that gathers the results' numbers). Job 1 adds the decisions record and the two S110 records that give Marletto's test; job 4 adds the decisions record and plain file 110 (for style). **No sandbox holds Avida's source or binary, or any raw run output**: those stay in the scratch space, and the build refuses any source outside `Semantics/`. There is no program in any sandbox (no `model/` folder), so the guard refuses every command: GLM may Read, Glob and Grep, and writes nothing. Each brief quotes the owner's words (S19, S20, S21, S23, S28, S43, S56, S57, S59) and asks for objections, each with **the exact fix**, terse, at most about 3,000 words, last line `END OF REPORT`. The briefs, manifests and job list are named, with their md5s, in `tools/s111x_jobs - S111, GLM cross-examination.json`, written by the build and committed before the launch.

- **The call**: glm-5.3 through Claude Code (S29), `--effort medium` (S17), the 1,000,000-token window, 6 attempts, at most 3 answers without END OF REPORT, 7,200 seconds per attempt, `--rule` (this file, committed and unchanged from HEAD), `--brief-md5`, `--manifest-md5`. Up to 3 passes per job. Sandboxes in `<scratchpad>/s111x_sandboxes/`, homes in `<scratchpad>/s111x_homes/`. Returns in `results/S111 Avida - GLM cross-examination returns/`.
- **Before the launch**: a dry test of the four sandboxes with a dummy key (built by the helper's own `build_sandbox`; the guard handed a write, `touch`, two `python3 -c`, `cat`, `env`, a redirect and a run of one of the S111 scripts, each to be refused; every sandbox to come back unchanged; no Avida binary, no `.spop` or `.dat` file, no file larger than the summaries), recorded and committed; S110's GLM run (session leader PID 6632) must have exited (`kill -0 6632` fails), so that no more than four GLM calls run at once.

## How the replies will be read

1. **Nothing is opened until all four calls end.** No reply, receipt, reasoning file, attempt file, stream file or guard log of this cross-examination is opened until every job has ended its last allowed pass: the run log holds `s111x_glm_loop: every pass ended; …` and `loop ended <UTC time>`, and the process in the pid file has exited. The progress lines may be watched; they hold no reply text. If a call is still running 24 hours after the launch, the runner may be stopped by its PID and the calls not ended recorded as not returned.
2. **What counts as a reply**: only `<tag>.response.txt` (or `<tag>_pass<k>.response.txt`); failed calls count neither way; connection failures are not answers; a key in the output or a sandbox not unchanged is reported before anything else is read.
3. **One Opus agent reads every objection and settles each**, by argument from the plan, the results, the scripts, the configuration and Avida's source, or **by rerunning** (Avida, the scripts, or a new check) in the scratch space, never in the repository; and records for each: the objection, its settlement (stands, stands in part, does not stand), the reason (or the rerun and its numbers), and what it changes. An objection is a claim until settled; an objection repeated by several jobs decides nothing (arguments, not numbers); silence is not agreement. The agent writes `results/S111 Avida - the GLM cross-examination, settled.md`, created at once and filled as it goes.
4. **Findings that stand amend the S111 files in corrected copies**: `… , after the cross-examination.md` (and `.json`) beside the results file, and corrected copies of any summary table or script that changes (a script's corrected copy gets its own plain name and note); the files as sent are kept as they were. The plain-words file 111 is updated to match, and its note says it now follows the check. Nothing in the theory's text, formal core, claims or program, any Part A, Part B or S110 file, the decisions record or `authority/` is written.
5. **The owner's words bind every finding as content** (S20 to S59). An objection that would settle for the owner something the S111 files leave open (whether these organisms hold knowledge; how the three properties should be read; what the explanation kind needs) is recorded, not applied (S28, S21). No finding ranks anything (S20).
6. **Records** follow the settlement, by the same agent: an addition to log S111 in the project story and the plain story, and Status, INDEX and README as earlier entries did. Then the owner chooses the next step.

## How the run is launched

From the repository root, after this file's commit is pushed and the build and dry test are committed, once `kill -0 6632` fails, one process, detached so that it outlives the agent that starts it, with the key loaded only into its own environment from the session's key file and never opened or printed by the agent, and the other keys unset:

```
setsid nohup bash -c 'cd /home/user/ThreadSmith || exit 1; echo "launched $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"; R="Semantics/results/S111 Avida - how the GLM cross-examination will be read, written before sending.md"; { git ls-files --error-unmatch -- "$R" >/dev/null && git diff --quiet HEAD -- "$R"; } || { echo "the reading rule is not committed or differs from HEAD; nothing sent"; exit 1; }; set -a; . <key file>; set +a; unset ATRIA_API_KEY MIMO_API_KEY OPENAI_API_KEY; python3 -B Semantics/tools/s111x_glm_loop.py "Semantics/tools/s111x_jobs - S111, GLM cross-examination.json"; echo "loop ended $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"' > <scratchpad>/s111x_glm_run.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
```

The process id of the session leader goes in `<scratchpad>/s111x_glm_run.pid`. The launching agent writes `results/S111 Avida - GLM cross-examination, launch record.md`, commits it, and hands back once the log shows all four calls sent.

## Unsure

- GLM cannot run Avida or see the raw output; it judges the numbers by their consistency with the scripts, the configuration and each other. A claim it cannot check is to be listed as not reached, not as an objection.
- GLM sees Avida's rules only as the build notes give them, with source lines; a rule misread there could pass unnoticed.
- One GLM job per angle may miss what the work also missed.

Decided by Claude under decisions S17, S29, S39, S56 and S59. 29 September 2026.

1	# S111 build notes, and Avida's rules as read from its source
2	
3	*Log S111. Written 29 September 2026 by the one Opus 5.5 agent of log S111. The Avida source and binary stay in the scratch space and are not in the repository; the lines below point into the source at commit 47f13dad (paths under `avida-core/`), so that a reader without the source can see which of Avida's rules the measures lean on. Short excerpts only.*
4	
5	## The build
6	
7	- Source: `github.com/devosoft/avida` at commit 47f13dad ("Merge pull request #95 from mmore500/whole-genome-duplication"), shallow clone; submodule `libs/apto` at its pinned commit 02e18980071d237f1ea4641f3f35cae469e2ed38, fetched with `git submodule update --init --depth 1 libs/apto`. `libs/backward-cpp` and `documentation` not fetched (not needed).
8	- Commands, in `avida/cbuild/`: `AVIDA_DISABLE_BACKTRACE=1 timeout 300 cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release ../` then `timeout 1800 nice make -j 3`. Both exited 0 (about 3 minutes). g++ 13.3.0, cmake 3.28.3, Ubuntu 24.04.
9	- **No patch and no extra compiler flag.** 285 compiler warnings (mostly the deprecated `std::binary_function`), no error. The only setting: the environment variable `AVIDA_DISABLE_BACKTRACE=1`, which Avida's own `build_avida` script uses as its fallback; it leaves out the backtrace library.
10	- Result: `cbuild/bin/avida`, "Avida 2.14.0, release build".
11	- One timing run before the plan was written: the default ancestor, seed 1, default settings, 3,000 updates in 104 seconds, 3,594 organisms at the end. Used only to choose run lengths.
12	- The analysis scripts use Python 3 and `numpy` (installed with `pip` for the alignment in `tools/s111_measure_the_worlds_over_time.py`).
13	
14	## Avida's rules the measures lean on
15	
16	| rule | where in the source | what it says |
17	|---|---|---|

1	# Error correction in constructor theory, and how the earlier attempts changed. In plain words
2	
3	*A note first. Written on 29 September 2026 by a Claude agent, for you, before GLM checked it; **it now follows the check**. GLM read the three records behind this page and raised 42 objections; another Claude agent weighed each one and corrected the records where it held (34 held, 7 held in part, 1 did not). This page was corrected to match the same day; section 6 says what the check changed. It uses none of the words you asked to be removed, except inside quotations. The corrected records are "Semantics/results/S110 Error correction from constructor theory's perspective, after the cross-examination.md", "Semantics/results/S110 The change map - the earlier frameworks and the present theory, after the cross-examination.md" (with a data file beside it) and "Semantics/results/S110 When something in a creative agent is knowledge - what the sources offer, after the cross-examination.md"; the versions GLM saw are kept beside them, and every objection and how it was weighed is in "Semantics/results/S110 - the GLM cross-examination, settled.md". Nothing in the theory was changed.*
4	
5	---
6	
7	## 1. What was found, and what it means for your question
8	
9	You asked, in effect: constructor theory already defines knowledge, so how do we tell when the vague, shapeless thing inside a creative agent counts as knowledge? Three findings bear on that.
10	
11	**First: in constructor theory, knowledge and error correction are tied at the root.** Constructor theory is the physics in Marletto's book: it describes the world by what changes can and cannot be made to happen. The book says knowledge is information that can keep itself in existence. It also says that the laws of physics preserve nothing complicated for free: anything complex wears away unless something keeps catching and fixing its errors. Put the two together and knowledge is information that gets its own errors fixed, either directly or through what it builds. A bacterium's DNA is the book's example: the cell that repairs each new copy of the DNA is itself built from that DNA.
12	
13	**Second: the book gives a definition and one test, but no way to apply them to a thought.** The test: knowledge is what you would have to wipe out, everywhere it has been copied, to stop something from being done reliably. The book applies it to a cricket's genes and a factory's plans, never to an idea in a head. And the book says outright that how knowledge is created by thinking is still an open problem, and asks, without answering, “What is it, exactly, that we have to store and error-correct?” (Marletto, ch. 7)
14	
15	**Third: your earlier frameworks already met the same wall, and took a position on it.** Two of them (FW3 and FW4) said that constructor theory's knowledge and knowledge that explains something are different kinds of thing and do not imply each other. Their examples: a mistaken idea that spreads by being repeated keeps itself in existence but explains nothing; an explanation that was worked out and then lost explained something but kept nothing. The next framework (FW5) objected that the examples mix up an idea, its copies, what can be done now, and what happened once, and put a bridge in its place: an explanation also counts as constructor-theory knowledge when it is kept going *because* of what it says. Then the bridge was dropped when the present theory was first written, and the word "knowledge" itself was removed in the clean-up of words you asked for. The present theory now has neither "information" nor "knowledge".
16	
17	**What this means for your question.** Constructor theory asks about the future of a piece of information (will it keep itself going?). Your frameworks, and the present theory, ask about the past of a problem (did something improve it?). Those are two different questions, and nothing written so far joins them except the dropped bridge. Checking FW3's two examples against the books shows each one rests on a reading. A mistaken idea that spreads is still knowledge on Deutsch's own account, but knowledge about the minds it lives in, not about what it says. Whether a lost explanation was knowledge depends on whether "able to keep itself in existence" means "in a suitable place" or "did in fact last". Nothing is settled here; those two readings are yours to weigh.
18	
19	## 2. Error correction, as the book gives it
20	
21	An example first. A mole cricket keeps its burrow's entrance round and clean. Marletto, as a child, kept stuffing it with grass; each day it was clear again. When the cricket left, her changes, and the rain's, were no longer undone, and the hole faded in a few days.
22	
23	- **The book never defines error correction.** The phrase appears five times in the whole book, in chapters 1, 2 and 7. What it gives is the need for it: without something that catches and fixes errors, anything complex falls apart. One of the five, in chapter 2, says that being able to test a theory's predictions is what makes correcting errors in science possible, and so makes science progress (the first version of the record missed this one).
24	- **Error correction is a job something keeps being able to do.** The book calls a thing that does a job and stays able to do it again a *catalyst*: a catalyst is something that makes a change happen and comes out unchanged, ready to do it again. The cricket is one; so is the cell that repairs DNA; so is a factory's repair crew.
25	- **Only information can be corrected this way.** To put something back, you must tell the damaged state from the right one, and copy the right one in. In the book, information is exactly what can be set to different states and copied. Deutsch adds that you cannot tell an error from a correct value at sight in anything smooth and continuous, which is why computers work in steps.
26	- **The book uses "error" in three ways.** For a copy, an error is a departure from the original (a monk's slip copying a manuscript). For natural selection there is no original: what fails is simply what does not survive (the book does not call that an error; putting it beside the other two is our step). For a thinker, an error is a flaw in an idea measured against a problem, and the problem can itself change. Only the third is what your theory calls criticism.
27	- **Knowledge can arise with no designer because error correction can.** Copying slips supply variety for free; the world weeds out what fails; and what survives builds its own repair. The book adds that thinking can make leaps that natural selection cannot.
28	- **On creative agents** the book says little: creativity is the ability to create new knowledge; human brains have it; how they do it, and whether a computer could, are open.
29	
30	## 3. The change map
31	
32	An example first. The idea that "a signal, a failure or a mismatch is not a criticism: a criticism says what is wrong and why" appears in the oldest framework and in every one after it, down to the present theory. The idea that "how many things an explanation reaches is a count you can go by" appears in one framework (FW3) and is gone by the next but one.
33	
34	A *change map* is a chart of how your attempts changed, one into the next: each idea in each version is a box, and each arrow says what happened to it next (kept, changed, added, dropped or replaced) and how sure that is.
35	
36	- **Size.** 185 boxes: from the oldest framework (FW0) 23, the software specification (I2) 15, FW2 35, FW3 25, FW4 20, FW5 32, the present theory 35. 145 arrows: 65 changed, 46 kept, 18 added, 10 dropped, 6 replaced. (Before the check: 172 boxes and 132 arrows; the check found ideas and links the first version had missed.)
37	- **How sure.** 48 arrows are stated by your frameworks themselves (their change lists or text), 18 by this project's own records, and **79 are Claude's reading**. Every arrow that crosses a missing document is Claude's reading. One arrow first marked as stated by FW5 turned out to be about an earlier version of the software specification than the one supplied, so it is now marked as Claude's reading.
38	- **Where the chain breaks.** Between the oldest framework and FW2 lie four documents that were not supplied. FW4 says itself that its link to FW3 is only "related". Between FW5 and the present theory lie four more missing documents, and then this project's own files.
39	- **What came through every version.** Newness is judged against what the thinker could already do. Credit for an idea needs an account of how it was built. A criticism says what is wrong and why. Predicting is not explaining. An idea is not the same as the ink or brain state that holds it. Creating something is not undone by losing it. No score, ranking or probability is put on explanations. Nothing is ever beyond criticism. (Some links in these chains are Claude's reading rather than arrows of the map; the corrected map now says which.)
40	- **What was tried and dropped.** A single basic "because" that everything else was built on (FW3; replaced in FW5). A way of preferring one explanation to another, and a count to do it with (FW3 and FW4; dropped in FW5). "Every learning of an idea is a creation of it" (FW3 and FW4; dropped in FW5). "Two layers of error correction", one fixing damaged copies and one fixing mistaken ideas (FW2; softened in FW5). The present theory has no passage on it, but it still keeps the two kinds of mistake apart: a thing can hold an idea faithfully while the idea itself is wrong about the world (the first version said it was simply gone).
41	- **Where information theory went.** Shannon's information theory, the mathematics of signals and noise, never entered any of them: none mentions it, and neither does Marletto's book. What did enter: a four-valued way of recording evidence (the oldest framework; gone by now); constructor theory's information (FW2 and FW5; the word dropped when the present theory was first written, but its machinery of possible and impossible jobs kept); constructor theory's knowledge (from the oldest framework to FW5; dropped); accounts of the mind as a prediction machine, used only as contrasts (FW2); and two ideas turned down outright, one that treats information as mere correlation and one that measures learning by expected information gain.
42	- **Twenty-one entries of named, missing documents (28 documents in all)**, among them the first version of the oldest framework's family, the three that did the groundwork for FW3 (including the one on "what knowledge cannot be"), the audit of FW3, and the audits of FW5. No gap was filled by guessing.
43	
44	## 4. Ways of telling when something is knowledge
45	
46	The sources offer eleven ways. Grouped, they come to four, and each starts from a different question. They are not ranked.
47	
48	1. **Does it keep itself going?** *Example:* a grandmother's bread recipe, copied by every grandchild who liked the bread, still baked seventy years later. This is constructor theory's definition, its "what would you have to wipe out" test, and its account of how a knot taught at a sailing club passes from hand to hand.
49	2. **Did it come from correcting errors?** *Example:* two people give the same train time; one checked the timetable against yesterday's delays, the other guessed. This is Deutsch's addition: knowledge hardly ever arises except by evolution or by thought, both of which correct errors.
50	3. **Did it improve a problem?** *Example:* a choir director hears the altos come in late, finds the conductor's gesture there is unclear, changes it, and the problem goes away without breaking anything else. This is what all six frameworks and the present theory ask, each in its own terms.
51	4. **Does it track something, with a history of how it came to?** *Example:* a frog snaps at small dark moving dots and catches flies, though nobody taught it. This is the present theory's notion of one thing standing for another; the theory never calls it knowledge, and it is set here beside the first question only because both need no one who knows.
52	
53	**One step comes before all of them**: saying which thing, held in what, looked at how closely. *Example:* before asking whether a cook's "feel for when a soufflé is ready" is knowledge, you must say where the feel lives (her eyes, her timing, a tap on the dish) and what it is about (this oven or any oven). Every source says this must be done; none says how to do it for a mind.
54	
55	## 5. What was read, what was not, and what is unsure
56	
57	- **Read in full**: Marletto's book, except the first half of chapter 2 and chapters 4 and 6, which were searched and read around each relevant passage, and the short stories between chapters, which were only searched. FW3 and FW4 in full; most of FW2 and FW5; the key parts of the oldest framework and the software specification; the parts of the present theory on carriers, criticism, building ideas, repair and physics. The earlier audit of the theory against the two books was built on, not redone.
58	- **From Deutsch's book**: only the passages Marletto leans on (knowledge, error correction, and ideas that spread by stopping criticism).
59	- **Not read**: the other books the frameworks cite, one of which you asked not to be opened; the missing documents.
60	- **Unsure**: 79 of the map's 145 arrows are Claude's reading; the two readings in section 1 (what a spreading mistaken idea is knowledge *of*; what "able to keep itself in existence" means) are Claude's, and the book states neither; which boxes belong to which theme is Claude's choice.
61	- **Every quotation from the books** was checked by a script against the books' text: each is word for word, at most 25 words, and none is run together with another. The books themselves are not in the repository.
62	
63	## 6. What the check changed
64	
65	GLM read the three records from four sides and raised 42 objections. Each was weighed on its argument, against the frameworks, the present theory and, for anything said about the books, the books' own text.
66	
67	- **The change map gained what it had missed**: 13 boxes (among them the oldest framework's way of saying an explanation is "good for now", and FW5's rule that dropping a premise makes an argument unusable without making its conclusion false) and 13 arrows, several of them stated by FW3's own change list. Several labels of who says what were corrected.
68	- **The list of what came through every version was honest only in part**: some of its steps were not arrows of the map. It now names each arrow, and marks the steps that are Claude's reading.
69	- **Two statements were too strong.** "Two layers of error correction" is not simply gone from the present theory (section 3 above). And the present theory does use the words "error correction", once, in the sentence that carries your footnote on premises taken as given.
70	- **One objection did not hold.** GLM objected that the record claimed too much in reporting the book as saying that every catalyst contains an "abstract catalyst" (the part made of knowledge). The book says exactly that, twice.
71	- **Nothing you left open was decided.** None of the objections chose between the two questions below or settled how to read "able to keep itself in existence".
72	
73	## 7. The next step
74	
75	You have already set it: your three properties of knowledge (it can cause itself to be copied, to resist change and to remain) are being measured on Avida's self-copying programs (log S111), with the kind of knowledge that explains coming next. Nothing in this check asks anything further of you before that work reports.
76

What did enter: a four-valued way of recording evidence (the oldest framework; gone by now); constructor theory's information (FW2 and FW5; the word dropped when the present theory was first written, but its machinery of possible and impossible jobs kept); constructor theory's knowledge (from the oldest framework to FW5; dropped); accounts of the mind as a prediction machine, used only as contrasts (FW2); and two ideas turned down outright, one that treats information as mere correlation and one that measures learning by expected information gain.
- **Twenty-one entries of named, missing documents (28 documents in all)**, among them the first version of the oldest framework's family, the three that did the groundwork for FW3 (including the one on "what knowledge cannot be"), the audit of FW3, and the audits of FW5. No gap was filled by guessing.

## 4. Ways of telling when something is knowledge

The sources offer eleven ways. Grouped, they come to four, and each starts from a different question. They are not ranked.

1. **Does it keep itself going?** *Example:* a grandmother's bread recipe, copied by every grandchild who liked the bread, still baked seventy years later. This is constructor theory's definition, its "what would you have to wipe out" test, and its account of how a knot taught at a sailing club passes from hand to hand.
2. **Did it come from correcting errors?** *Example:* two people give the same train time; one checked the timetable against yesterday's delays, the other guessed. This is Deutsch's addition: knowledge hardly ever arises except by evolution or by thought, both of which correct errors.
3. **Did it improve a problem?** *Example:* a choir director hears the altos come in late, finds the conductor's gesture there is unclear, changes it, and the problem goes away without breaking anything else. This is what all six frameworks and the present theory ask, each in its own terms.
4. **Does it track something, with a history of how it came to?** *Example:* a frog snaps at small dark moving dots and catches flies, though nobody taught it. This is the present theory's notion of one thing standing for another; the theory never calls it knowledge, and it is set here beside the first question only because both need no one who knows.

**One step comes before all of them**: saying which thing, held in what, looked at how closely. *Example:* before asking whether a cook's "feel for when a soufflé is ready" is knowledge, you must say where the feel lives (her eyes, her timing, a tap on the dish) and what it is about (this oven or any oven). Every source says this must be done; none says how to do it for a mind.

## 5. What was read, what was not, and what is unsure

- **Read in full**: Marletto's book, except the first half of chapter 2 and chapters 4 and 6, which were searched and read around each relevant passage, and the short stories between chapters, which were only searched. FW3 and FW4 in full; most of FW2 and FW5; the key parts of the oldest framework and the software specification; the parts of the present theory on carriers, criticism, building ideas, repair and physics. The earlier audit of the theory against the two books was built on, not redone.
- **From Deutsch's book**: only the passages Marletto leans on (knowledge, error correction, and ideas that spread by stopping criticism).
- **Not read**: the other books the frameworks cite, one of which you asked not to be opened; the missing documents.
- **Unsure**: 79 of the map's 145 arrows are Claude's reading; the two readings in section 1 (what a spreading mistaken idea is knowledge *of*; what "able to keep itself in existence" means) are Claude's, and the book states neither; which boxes belong to which theme is Claude's choice.
- **Every quotation from the books** was checked by a script against the books' text: each is word for word, at most 25 words, and none is run together with another. The books themselves are not in the repository.

GLM read the three records from four sides and raised 42 objections. Each was weighed on its argument, against the frameworks, the present theory and, for anything said about the books, the books' own text.

X4.5: knockout example mechanism story ("runs, makes room, and never fills it") presented as observed; not in results. Fix: rephrase to what was measured or attribute to what the step does.
X4.6: "writes a random instruction instead" — can be the same instruction (results/build notes say so); "instead" overstates. Fix wording.
X4.7: generations rounded two ways in one file (16,000 vs 15,900); also "the simplest sum, NOT" is not in the results (results say only "the hardest, EQU"). Fix: use one rounding; say "NOT, the simplest of the nine" only if... fix: "For NOT, one of the simplest sums, about a fifth..." Hmm exact fix: "For the sum NOT, about a fifth of the programs still did it afterwards".

Wait — also double-check X4.4 wording: plain "The first try of four control runs failed from a missing line break in a file and was run again." Results: "the first attempt of K2, K3 and K4 failed at once ('Unknown instruction nop-X': the added line ran onto the last line of the instruction file...), and K1 ran without nop-X defined; nothing from that attempt is used. Fixed in the scripts, and all five controls rerun." So: three failed from the line break; K1 ran (wrongly) for another reason; five rerun. Plain says four failed from the line break. Inaccurate in count and cause. Fix: "The first try of the control runs went wrong (three stopped at once from a missing line break in a file; the fourth ran without the switch-off instruction in it); nothing from it was used, and all five controls were run again."

Also check plain section 7 first sentence: "Tested: the three properties, as set out in the plan written before anything was run; the controls; Marletto's test on the sums." ✓.

Now word count of report — keep terse.

Also (b) checked-no-objection list: numbers in sections 1–6 and 8 (15/85 knockouts; 389 steps; rates 1/400, 1/133, 1/50; 69/40/13 fidelity; 10,000 random programs; K1 66, K2 65, K3 2,000, K4 500; 69–79% viable and 21–31%; 14–19% and 27–36% neutral with every high above every low; 84%/18%; 54-of-54 across six moments; copy loop gone by 20,000 in six runs; 3,481 minimum; 0 identical; 0–49% copy loop at high; 58–84%; 65–86%; EQU six of nine; 26 instructions, 1.4 points, 44 of 3,600 (consistent); 1%–4%; 93–100%; 19–26; NOT ~fifth, up to 46%; departures/not-tested/unsure lists; S23 words none; S21/S28 respected; marked pre-check; one next step; one-word-per-thing; style beside file 110.

(c) not reached: raw run output not present (numbers judged only against summary tables and .json — consistency confirmed); the exact dominant count 44 for low seed2 not in summaries; Avida source not present (rules taken from build notes).

One more scan: does the plain file anywhere misuse "the same" numbers? Section 4: "at the end of a low-rate run, 84% of the programs (on average over the three runs) still had the first program's instruction at the places of the 15 copying instructions" — "at the end of a low-rate run... on average over the three runs" — slight tension ("a run" vs average over three runs) but it says average. Fine.

Also section 5: "in 0% to 49% at the high rate" ✓ (0, 0.0008, 0.4873 → 0.00008%? 0.0008 = 0.08%, rounds to 0% ✓).

Also section 1 bullet Remains: "even its copying instructions were rewritten into a faster version" ✓.

OK. One more: does the plain file state the world rewards sums with "more running time" — section 6 ✓; matches results ("pays for it in processor time").

Also — "Avida's usual" for default rate ✓ results call it "Avida's own".

I'm fairly confident in the objection list. Let me also double-check the claim in X4.1 about expected from rates alone: (1−0.0025)^100 = e^{−0.25}≈0.7787. Observed 0.693. So indeed not "close" — the plain sentence's "close to what the rates alone lead one to expect" would be false for a reader computing from the plain file's own information. Good.

Also should I mention that section 2's mutation description omits that these ins/del apply "at each split" — covered.

Also, X4.2's severity: the plain reader believes switching off copy errors alone freezes the population — a substantive misreading of what the no-mutation control shows. Yes, serious-ish, second.

Now write the report. Format: (a) objections table, most serious first; (b) one line; (c) not reached lines. Last line exactly END OF REPORT.
